title: Liberal jurisprudence on bigamy
primary_topics: Bigamy under the Revised Penal Code and earlier rulings requiring a prior judicial declaration of nullity before the invalidity of a first marriage could be a defense
Pulido v. People (2021, en banc, unanimous) -- a prior void ab initio marriage is a valid defense without a judicial declaration; reiterated in Lapira v. Fariscal (Feb. 26, 2026, Third Division)
Lapira facts -- Imelda Lapira married Jimmy Fariscal in 2001 but had a 2000 marriage record with Takahiko Sato, which she called a 'sham' for entry into Japan; convicted by the RTC and CA

Three holdings -- Article 40 requires a declaration only for remarriage and allows collateral attack; a marriage certificate is prima facie evidence rebuttable by substantial evidence (LCR certification that no certificate or license was issued); a purely civil matter not touching the sacrament
Principles -- courts cannot impose criminal penalties on a marital bond that was 'nothing but a phantom'; a prior declaration of nullity is still needed to remarry
Closing -- the rulings respect the constitutional inviolability of marriage and Church doctrine while freeing the innocent from a void union

stances.claim: Pulido v. People modified earlier jurisprudence so that a prior void ab initio marriage is a valid defense to bigamy without a prior judicial declaration, and Lapira v. Fariscal reiterated it.
Article 40 of the Family Code requires a declaration of nullity only for remarriage and does not bar an accused from collaterally attacking a void prior marriage.
A marriage certificate is prima facie evidence that may be rebutted by substantial evidence, such as a Local Civil Registrar certification that no certificate or license was issued.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban explains a liberal shift in bigamy jurisprudence. Bigamy under the Revised Penal Code is contracting a second marriage while a valid first marriage exists; earlier rulings barred offending spouses from remarrying and from using the invalidity of a prior marriage as a defense without a prior judicial declaration of nullity. In Pulido v. People (2021), a unanimous en banc Court held that a prior void ab initio marriage is a valid defense even without such a declaration, and Lapira v. Fariscal (Feb. 26, 2026) reiterated this in acquitting a woman convicted below. Imelda Lapira married Jimmy Fariscal in 2001, but a record showed she had married Japanese national Takahiko Sato in 2000; she said that marriage was a sham arranged for her entry into Japan, with no ceremony and only a blank paper she signed for 'Jo.' The trial court convicted her and the Court of Appeals affirmed because the first marriage had not been declared void. The Supreme Court ruled on three points. First, Article 40 of the Family Code requires a declaration of nullity only for remarriage and allows collateral attack on a void prior marriage; Imelda's marriage to Sato lacked a license and ceremony. Second, a marriage certificate is prima facie evidence rebuttable by substantial evidence, here a Local Civil Registrar certification that it issued no certificate and no license was applied for. Third, the matter was purely civil: no sacramental union was involved. A declaration of nullity is still required to remarry. CJP says courts should not impose criminal penalties on a bond that was nothing but a phantom, and that the rulings respect both the constitutional inviolability of marriage and Church doctrine, balancing reverence for matrimony with criminal justice.
